question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what ingredient do the authors add once the soap has completely melted in the traditional remelting method?
supporting_passage:
When all the soap is molten, additions of pearl ash
solution are made to give it a finer and smoother texture, render it
more transparent, and increase its lathering properties.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what hot-air temperature do the authors specify for drying chipped soap before milling?
reference_answer: The chipped soap is exposed to hot air at 95-105 deg. F. (35-40 deg. C.).
supporting_passage:
Cutting the soap into bars or strips and open
piling greatly facilitates the drying, which is usually effected by
chipping the soap and exposing it on trays to a current of hot air at
95-105 deg. F. (35-40 deg. C.).

section: (ii.) Milling and Incorporation of Colour, Perfume or Medicament.
question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, when preparing the finest milled toilet soaps, at what point do the authors advise adding perfume?
reference_answer: They advise introducing perfume after the colour has been thoroughly mixed throughout the mass.
required_key_points: after the colour has been thoroughly mixed throughout the mass
supporting_passage:
A better
plan, however, especially in the case of the best grade soaps, where the
perfumes added are necessarily more delicate and costly, is to make the
addition of the perfume when the colour has been thoroughly mixed
throughout the mass.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what outlet temperature do the authors recommend for the plodder when forming a bar of milled soap?
reference_answer: They heat the plodder nozzle to about 120 deg. or 130 deg. F. (49 deg.-55 deg. C.).
required_key_points: about 120 deg. or 130 deg. F. (49 deg.-55 deg. C.)
supporting_passage:
The nozzle of the plodder
is heated by means of a Bunsen burner to about 120 deg. or 130 deg. F.
(49 deg.-55 deg. C.) to allow the soap to be easily forced out, and this
also imparts a good gloss and finish to the ejected bar--if the nozzle
is too hot, however, the soap will be blistered, whereas insufficient
heat will result in streaky soap of a poor and dull appearance.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what tablet-weight range do the authors give for an adjustable band or collar mould?
reference_answer: The mould can stamp tablets from 2 ozs. to 5-1/3 ozs.
supporting_passage:
In this form (Fig, 27) the mould may be
adjusted to stamp various sized tablets, say from 2 ozs. to 5-1/3 ozs.
and different impressions given by means of removable die plates.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what practical soap-stock formula did Unna find most successful for preparing medicinal soap?
reference_answer: His preferred base combined one part of olive oil with eight parts of beef tallow, was saponified with two parts of soda to one part of potash, and retained 3 or 4 per cent. unsaponified fat.
required_key_points: one part of olive oil with eight parts of beef tallow
two parts of soda to one part of potash
supporting_passage:
The preparation of medicinal soaps appears to have been first taken up
in a scientific manner by Unna of Hamburg in 1886, who advocated the use
of soap in preference to plasters as a vehicle for the application of
certain remedies.

Theoretically, he considered a soap-stock made entirely from beef tallow
the most suitable for the purpose, but in practice found that the best
results were obtained by using a superfatted soap made from a blend of
one part of olive oil with eight parts of beef tallow, saponified with a
mixture of two parts of soda to one part of potash, sufficient fat being
employed to leave an excess of 3 or 4 per cent. unsaponified.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what patented name was given to the altered borax salt proposed for incorporation into soap?
reference_answer: The neutral mono-borate of soda was named "Kastilis".
supporting_passage:
As a remedy for this it has been proposed to add
sufficient alkali to convert the borax into neutral mono-borate of soda
which is then added to the soap. This process is patented and the name
"Kastilis" has been given to the neutral salt.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, to what moisture percentage do the authors recommend drying soap before adding a larger amount of glycerine by milling?
reference_answer: They recommend drying the soap to 9 or 10 per cent. moisture before milling in the glycerine.
supporting_passage:
The best way is to dry the soap somewhat further than
usual, till it contains say only 9 or 10 per cent. moisture and then
mill in the glycerine.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what exact mixture do the authors recommend to make the aroma of thymol soap more agreeable?
reference_answer: They recommend 2-1/2 per cent. of thymol crystals and 1-1/2 per cent. of a good red thyme oil.
required_key_points: 1-1/2 per cent. of a good red thyme oil
supporting_passage:
It is preferable to replace part of the thymol with red thyme oil,
the thymene of which imparts a sweeter odour to the soap than if
produced with thymol alone. A suitable blend is 2-1/2 per cent. of
thymol crystals and 1-1/2 per cent. of a good red thyme oil.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what percentage weight difference do the authors report between otherwise identically sized floating-soap tablets before and after aeration?
reference_answer: They report a 10 per cent. difference in weight.
supporting_passage:
The
difference in weight of a tablet of the same size before and after
aerating amounts to 10 per cent.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, for calico-printing work involving dyes that would be harmed by hot washing, which soap do the authors say is used on the most expensive goods?
reference_answer: They specify a neutral olive-oil soft soap.
supporting_passage:
A
neutral olive-oil soft soap, owing to its solubility in cold water, may
be used for fibres coloured with most delicate dyes, which would be
fugitive in hot soap solutions, and this soap is employed for the most
expensive work.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, why do the authors insist that soap for silk dyeing contain no rosin?
reference_answer: The soap may undergo decomposition in the acid dye bath, and the liberated rosin acids cling to the silk fibres.
required_key_points: decomposition in the acid dye bath
liberated rosin acids cling to the silk fibres
supporting_passage:
It is essential, however, that the soap should be
free from rosin on account of its frequent use and consequent
decomposition in the acid dye bath, when any liberated rosin acids would
cling to the silk fibres and produce disagreeable results.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what range of siliceous matter content do the authors assign to polishing soaps?
reference_answer: They state that polishing soaps often contain from 85 to 90 per cent. siliceous matter.
supporting_passage:
Soap powders or dry soaps are powdered mixtures of soap, soda ash, or
soda crystals, and other chemicals, whilst polishing soaps often contain
from 85 to 90 per cent. siliceous matter, and can scarcely be termed
soap.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, how do the authors account for the characteristic colour developed by old-fashioned Brown Windsor soap?
reference_answer: Through age and frequent remelting, oxidation of the fatty acids gave the originally curd-based Brown Windsor soap its brown tint.
supporting_passage:
The old-fashioned Brown Windsor soap was originally a curd
soap that with age and frequent remelting had acquired a brown tint by
oxidation of the fatty acids--the oftener remelted the better the
resultant soap.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, how does the Cressonnieres drying apparatus seek to prevent a hard crust from developing on soap shavings?
reference_answer: It places milling rollers among the drying belts to alter which soap surfaces are exposed to the air.
required_key_points: milling rollers among the drying belts
alter which soap surfaces are exposed to the air
supporting_passage:
In the Cressonnieres' system, where the shavings of chilled soap are
dried by being carried through a heated chamber upon a series of endless
bands (the first discharging the contents on to a lower belt which
projects at the end, and is moving in the opposite direction, and so
on), this is performed by intercepting milling rollers in the system of
belts (Eng. Pat. 4,916, 1898) whereby the surfaces exposed to the drying
are altered, and it is claimed that the formation of hardened crust is
prevented.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what method did Ehrhardt patent for incorporating a mercury medicament into antiseptic soap?
reference_answer: Ehrhardt used mercury albuminate, introducing it into the soap in an alkaline solution.
required_key_points: into the soap in an alkaline solution
supporting_passage:
Ehrhardt (Eng. Pat. 2,407, 1898) patented a method of making
antiseptic mercury soap by using mercury albuminate--a combination of
mercuric chloride and casein, which is soluble in alkali, and added to
the soap in an alkaline solution.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, which traditional soap types do the authors recommend for scouring lower-grade wool when their first-choice soap is too expensive?
reference_answer: They recommend old-fashioned curd mottled soap or curd soaps boiled very dry.
supporting_passage:
The high price of olive-oil soap, however, renders its use prohibitive
for lower class goods, and in such cases no better soap can be suggested
than the old-fashioned curd mottled or curd soaps (boiled very dry), as
free as possible from uncombined caustic alkali.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, how did Stockhausen claim his Monopole Soap behaved differently from ordinary soap during textile dyeing?
reference_answer: He claimed that it was not precipitated in the dye-bath and was not deposited upon the fibres.
supporting_passage:
Stockhausen (Eng. Pat. 24,868, 1897) makes
special claim for a soap, termed Monopole Soap, to be used in place of
Turkey-red oils in the dyeing and printing of cotton goods and finishing
of textile fabrics. The soap is prepared by heating the sulphonated oil
(obtained on treatment of castor oil with sulphuric acid) with alkali,
and it is stated that the product is not precipitated when used in the
dye-bath as is ordinary soap, nor is it deposited upon the fibres.
